drills.q: What is the central design decision when authoring an MCP server?
drills.a: Tool granularity -- neither too fine (ORM-shaped) nor too coarse (a god-tool with an action string).

drills.q: What is the linguistic tell of a too-fine tool set?
drills.a: Naming a tool requires 'and' -- it's doing an assembly/join step the caller's code should have done.

drills.q: What is the linguistic tell of a too-coarse tool (a god-tool)?
drills.a: Naming it requires 'or' -- a decision got hidden inside a string argument instead of the tool boundary.

drills.q: At roughly what tool count does selection accuracy start collapsing, per 2026 benchmark data?
drills.a: Around 20 tools accuracy is still ~19/20; by ~107 tools it approaches complete failure. A pooled unfiltered catalogue scored 13.62% in one stress test.

drills.q: GitHub Copilot cut its tool count from 40 to 13. What did it gain?
drills.a: A ~400ms latency reduction and a 2-5 percentage point accuracy improvement on the same tasks.

drills.q: List the three fixes for tool-selection collapse, cheapest first.
drills.a: Namespace by service prefix; curate to real workflows instead of auto-wrapping every endpoint; progressive disclosure (list_capabilities/invoke) or topic-scoped sub-servers.

drills.q: Why should a tool never accept a secret as an argument?
drills.a: The model holds the value in its own context and can echo it into a later call, a log, or its final response. Read secrets server-side at call time instead.

drills.q: Explain the difference in purpose between dry_run and an idempotency key on a mutating tool.
drills.a: dry_run previews the effect before it happens, for trust and plan verification. An idempotency key makes a retried call return the stored result instead of double-executing. They solve different problems and neither substitutes for the other.

drills.q: Derive an idempotency key for a tool call and name the common bug in doing so.
drills.a: hash(session_id, tool_name, sorted(args)). Common bug: not sorting the args, so logically identical calls with differently-ordered keys hash differently and the mechanism silently fails.

drills.q: Where should a tool's failure be surfaced in an MCP response, and what breaks if you get it wrong?
drills.a: As isError:true content in the tools/call result, never a raw JSON-RPC protocol error. Getting it wrong raises a client-side exception that kills the whole run instead of giving the model something to react to.

drills.q: What are the two separate evals needed to validate an MCP server, and what does each expose?
drills.a: Selection accuracy (right tool, valid args -- exposes granularity problems) and task success (right outcome -- exposes schema/error-message problems). A server can pass one and fail the other.

drills.q: When is building an MCP server the wrong call for an internal tool?
drills.a: When exactly one agent in one process will ever call it -- a direct function call is faster and has no schema/subprocess/network overhead, and MCP earns its cost only with a genuinely different consumer.
